question:
In an algebra laboratory, students investigate how a matrix can be changed systematically through elementary transformations. They begin with $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\2&5&1\\3&7&2\end{bmatrix}$. The teacher explains that permitted transformations include interchanging two rows or columns, multiplying a row or column by a non-zero scalar, and adding to one row or column a scalar multiple of another. The students first perform two row transformations successively and then study a row interchange. To compare row and column transformations, they finally return to the original matrix $A$ and perform a column transformation independently.

(a) Apply $R_2\rightarrow R_2-2R_1$ to $A$ and obtain matrix $B$.

(b) Starting from $B$, apply $R_3\rightarrow R_3-3R_1$ and obtain matrix $C$.

(c) Apply $R_2\leftrightarrow R_3$ to $C$, find the resulting matrix and identify the type of elementary transformation used.

(d) Starting again from the original matrix $A$, apply $C_2\rightarrow C_2+2C_1$. Find the resulting matrix and justify why the operation is an elementary column transformation.
explanation:
(a)
The transformation is $R_2\rightarrow R_2-2R_1$. The new second row is $[2,5,1]-2[1,2,-1]=[2,5,1]-[2,4,-2]=[0,1,3]$. Therefore, $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\3&7&2\end{bmatrix}$. This transformation adds a scalar multiple of one row to another row.

(b)
Starting with $B$, apply $R_3\rightarrow R_3-3R_1$. The new third row is $[3,7,2]-3[1,2,-1]=[3,7,2]-[3,6,-3]=[0,1,5]$. Hence, $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\0&1&5\end{bmatrix}$.

(c)
The transformation $R_2\leftrightarrow R_3$ interchanges the second and third rows. Therefore, the resulting matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&5\\0&1&3\end{bmatrix}$. The operation used is an elementary row interchange.

(d)
For the original matrix $A$, $C_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{bmatrix}$ and $C_2=\begin{bmatrix}2\\5\\7\end{bmatrix}$. Under $C_2\rightarrow C_2+2C_1$, the new second column is $\begin{bmatrix}2\\5\\7\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\\9\\13\end{bmatrix}$. Thus, the transformed matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&4&-1\\2&9&1\\3&13&2\end{bmatrix}$. Since a scalar multiple of one column has been added to another column, this is an elementary column transformation.

options.A:
(a) $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&-1\\3&7&2\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&-1\\0&1&5\end{bmatrix}$.
(c) Interchanging $R_2$ and $R_3$ is an elementary row interchange.
(d) $\begin{bmatrix}1&4&-1\\2&9&1\\3&13&2\end{bmatrix}$.
options.B:
(a) $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\3&7&2\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\0&1&5\end{bmatrix}$.
(c) The resulting matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\0&1&5\end{bmatrix}$; this is row scaling.
(d) $\begin{bmatrix}1&4&-1\\2&9&1\\3&13&2\end{bmatrix}$.
options.C:
(a) $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\3&7&2\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\0&1&5\end{bmatrix}$.
(c) $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&5\\0&1&3\end{bmatrix}$ is obtained by row interchange.
(d) $C_2\rightarrow C_2+2C_1$ gives $\begin{bmatrix}1&3&-1\\2&7&1\\3&10&2\end{bmatrix}$.
options.D:
(a) $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\3&7&2\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&3\\0&1&5\end{bmatrix}$.
(c) $R_2\leftrightarrow R_3$ gives $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\\0&1&5\\0&1&3\end{bmatrix}$ and is an elementary row interchange.
(d) $C_2\rightarrow C_2+2C_1$ gives $\begin{bmatrix}1&4&-1\\2&9&1\\3&13&2\end{bmatrix}$ and is an elementary column transformation.
